catalog_quote: 3.3 Stress Patterns A very important aspect of any language, and one rarely if ever represented in spelling, is the stress or intonation pattern. The Cree stress pattern differs considerably from that of English and can present many problems for the non-speaker, especially since stress is not overtly marked in Cree spelling. ... 3.3.1 2-Syllable Words In two-syllable words, the final (or ultimate) syllable is typically given the main stress: ... wacask {wuh TSUSK} “muskrat” atim {uh TIM} “dog” ... 3.3.2 3-(or more)-Syllable Words In words of three or more syllables, the third last (or antepenultimate) syllable receives the main stress, while the final syllable also receives some secondary stress: maskisin {MUSS kiss SIN} “moccasin; shoe” maskisina {muss KISS sin NUH} “moccasins; shoes” ... In contrast, antepenultimate stress does hold in Cree regardless of the length of the vowel of the…

At minimum add a dialect-transfer caution and Cook 1991 to sources now, and resolve the plai1258/swam1239 inconsistency (same Okimasis-Wolvengrey antepenult rule codes Swampy 'fixed' while Plains is 'excluded').

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation is verbatim at the stated place in the extracted text we hold of Okimasis & Wolvengrey 2008 (sec. 3.3, pp. 11-12). (2) Deciding source: a 2008 SRO spelling manual that calls itself 'this Plains Cree manual' and scopes its stress footnote to 'the Plains Cree pronunciation'; it is not a description of Swampy Cree, the languoid of this key. Glottolog's top descriptive works for swam1239 are Ellis 1983 (713 pp) and Ellis 1962/2000, none held or openly reachable (archive.org borrow-only, FTS blocked again today). (3) downloaded now: Cook 1991 (open, Algonquian Conference) quotes Ellis 1983:36 for west-James-Bay Cree: stress non-distinctive, with marked degrees of stress recorded 'as an aid to memory', and Cook reads Ellis's marked text as 'unpredictable, although the strongest stress is quite frequently on the antepenultimate' -- this refines rather than confirms

sources.quote: Data are Plains Cree (northern Alberta). Quotes Ellis 1983:36 on west-coast-of-James-Bay (Swampy/Moose) Cree: 'In Cree, stress is non-distinctive ... There are, however, clearly marked degrees of stress; and ... these have been marked as an aid to memory' with acute = strongest, grave = next strongest. Cook: 'From the stress marked by Ellis in the text on page 71, stress is indeed unpredictable, although the strongest stress is quite frequently on the antepenultimate syllable' and 'although stress is considered nondistinctive, it is unpredictable and has to be marked'. For his Plains data Cook
sources.locator: pp. 21-22 (Ellis 1983:36 quoted verbatim on p. 22); rule summary (8) p. 24, (14) p. 27
sources.note: Open; quotes Ellis 1983:36 verbatim and characterises Ellis's Swampy/Moose stress marking as 'unpredictable, although.. quite frequently on the antepenultimate'; should be added to the record's sources as the reachable witness for the Swampy primary.

sources.note: The listed open URL (cs.chalmers.se/~harald2/grammars/) is dead: it redirects to a Plesk default page on haraldhammarstrom.ruhosting.nl, and the same path on that host returns 404. Because the work is public domain (1875), the archive.org copy lectureongrammat00hunt (University of Toronto scan, unrestricted) was downloaded instead and read; the quotes above are from that copy. Hunter is a 19th-century missionary grammar (lecture of 1862 plus verb paradigms) with no phonology section beyond the orthography key; it neither confirms nor contradicts the catalog's antepenultimate rule.
